title: Site hero identity experiments 2026
summary: Working doc for new homepage hero directions that lean into engineering guarantees (latency & cost control) while testing more human, product-oriented metaphors. Contains micro-copy, experiment matrix, competitive signals, and open questions for alignment with product/eng before formal A/B tests.
hero_variants: Ship predictable AI: low-latency, cost-aware inference that scales with you
Inference you can trust — production latency, developer simplicity
Stop trading speed for cost. Serve reliably, optimize relentlessly.
The inference runtime engineers actually want — fast, observable, and accountable
hero_rationale: Goal: move beyond abstract promises ("fast and cheap") to a claim that combines tangible levers (latency SLOs, reserved capacity, and cost controls) with emotional reassurance (trust, predictability). Each variant tests a different balance: product-first metaphor vs engineering assurance vs economic control.
supporting_bullets: Hosted API + Dedicated + Private: same SDK, different isolation and SLAs
Pin versions, canary rollouts, automatic fallback to cheaper variants
Real-time cost & latency breakdowns in Console; token-level visibility
Smart routing: route by latency, cost, or compliance policy
microcopy_ctas: Get started in 5 minutes — try hosted API
product_page_headlines: Route, cache, quantize — control unit economics without rewriting your stack
From playground to SLA: rollout controls that match product risk
experiment_hypotheses: H1: 'Predictable' language will lift signups from platform engineers who value SLAs more than raw throughput.
H2: A/B with 'Engineer-first' vs 'Business-econ' hero will show different activation funnels: engineers -> API keys; PMs -> cost estimator.
H3: Adding a short trust line (SLA + dedicated option) increases Demo requests from enterprise by 12% in week-over-week tests.
experiment_matrix_notes: Planned matrix: hero variant x trust line (SLA+Dedicated vs product features) x CTA (signup vs sales). Measure: signup->first-call, Demo requests, time-to-first-invoke. Run 2 weeks per cell with traffic allocation 10/10/10/remaining to baseline.
competitive_notes: Competitive signals updated Nov 2025: Major API providers are emphasizing model access and safety. Three small inference runtimes market themselves on cost. Our angle: unify predictability + economics + rollout controls. Risk: copy that sounds 'infra-y' will alienate product leads. Opportunity: technical proof points (trace screenshots, latency distribution) translate to trust among SRE/platform buyers.
ux_animation_scripts: Frame 1: global map with regional routing pulses -> text: 'Serve where your users are', fades to\n
Frame 2: small stack diagram showing SDK -> smart router -> model variants -> text: 'Same API, different guarantees', pulses
Frame 3: token cost meter animates while latency histogram tightens -> text: 'Control cost without sacrificing SLAs'
accessibility_notes: All hero animations must have reduced-motion alternative. Provide ARIA labels for the latency histogram and ensure contrast ratios for microcopy CTAs meet AA. Text alternatives: concise hero string and 2-line explainer.
open_questions: Which engineering proof points are acceptable public-facing? (trace screenshots, exact p95 numbers?)
Should we call out 'quantized models' explicitly or keep model internals high-level?
Do legal/privacy want an explicit line about data residency under Private?
What is the SLA blurb length that legal approves for hero area?

body:
Draft notes and copy experiments

Overview:
This doc collects hero variants and playtest notes focused on making the homepage perform for engineering buyers without losing product-level clarity. The core tension: talk about systems (SLOs, batching, quantization) vs outcomes (predictable cost, uptime, developer velocity).

Quick playbook:
- Primary claim: single concise sentence that commits to one tangible thing (predictable latency, cost controls, or easy rollouts).
- Secondary line: one-sentence elaboration with specific levers (dedicated pools, canary rollouts, token-level cost).
- CTA: choose either 'Get started' or 'Talk to sales' depending on traffic cohort.

Variant testing notes:
- Keep baseline copy in experiments so we can revert quickly.
- Tag experiments in GTM-729 and track by cohort (self-serve vs enterprise).
- Capture scroll maps and heatmaps for each hero variant.

Competitive posture details:
- We should avoid directly naming competitors but call out where we differ: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private and deterministic controls over cost and latency.

Final thought:
Make sure the hero supports downstream pages: product pages need longer, more technical proofs and diagrams. The homepage hero is shorthand: pick the single strongest buyer-oriented promise and test it fast.
